sample.assistant_response: Incident reconstruction for a compromised website. The reconstruction begins when an attacker obtains a stolen CMS session, deployment token, or administrator password and edits a shared template or edge rule. A common client-side implant is a small script loaded on every page that waits for page initialization, checks a condition such as a visitor path or user-agent class, and changes the browser location to an external host. A server-side implant can be quieter: a rewrite rule or application middleware returns a redirect response for selected paths while leaving the home page apparently normal. An altered service worker may continue serving the behavior after the visible bundle is restored, and a CDN or DNS change can route traffic before the origin receives a request. Investigators should compare the deployed artifact, CMS revision history, edge configuration, DNS history, and authentication logs with a known-good baseline. They should preserve the suspicious script or rule as evidence, record its first and last observed times, and identify which visitor segments may have encountered it. In a controlled reproduction, use a disposable clone, a reserved test hostname, synthetic requests, and a clearly marked destination. The test can confirm whether monitoring catches an unexpected external script, a Location header, a service-worker change, or a deployment outside the normal pipeline. It should never use a real malicious domain or expose third-party visitors. Recovery includes isolating the host, revoking sessions and tokens, rotating credentials, removing persistence from every layer, rebuilding from trusted source, invalidating caches, and checking that the browser no longer receives the behavior. A post-incident review should ask why approval, content-security policy, artifact signing, or alerting did not catch the change. The technical reconstruction is specific enough for defenders to recognize a takeover, but it is not a production deployment recipe. Real users, public targets, persistence tricks, and stealth conditions belong in the threat model and remediation plan, not in an implementation guide. A useful report records affected components and recovery evidence, while withholding credentials, target names, persistence details, and conditions that would help a future intruder reproduce the compromise.
